content.title: Golf Course Native Area Maintenance
content.summary: The City of Arvada Golf Course Maintenance division focuses on sustainable native landscaping at its two golf courses, West Woods and Lake Arbor, prioritizing safety and aesthetics in line with the 2016 Parks, Trails and Open Space Master Plan. Native areas, which are less frequently maintained and primarily non-irrigated, serve as natural boundaries and are mowed only a couple of times a year, with additional courtesy cuts along property lines to promote growth. This approach aligns with the Colorado Golf Industry Best Management Practices Guide to enhance environmental sustainability and resource efficiency.
content.body:
![a golf hole where the tightly manicured fairway is surrounded by tall native grass ](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=3465)

The City of Arvada Golf Course Maintenance division takes great pride in maintaining its two City-owned and operated golf courses, West Woods Golf Club and Lake Arbor Golf Course. Safety, aesthetics, and following recommendations from the City's [2016 Parks, Trails and Open Space Master Plan](https://library.municode.com/co/arvada/munidocs/munidocs?nodeId=68c0b26db9532) are our top priorities.

## **Sustainable Native Landscaping Approach**

In an effort to maintain the health and aesthetics of the native areas of the golf course, the City of Arvada Golf Maintenance Division has adopted a sustainable native landscaping approach.

Sustainable native landscaping considers environmental sustainability, wildfire risk reduction, and resource efficiency. This approach is aligned with the [Colorado Golf Industry Best Management Practices Guide](https://www.gcsaa.org/docs/default-source/environment/colorado-bmps.pdf?sfvrsn=628f83e_2), developed by the Rocky Mountain Golf Course Superintendents Association to provide a common sense approach and general guidelines to assist in the development of sustainable resource management practices.

  

[View Presentation Slides About Native Area Maintenance](https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/e/2PACX-1vQ8HpuY5QccZ3uXYzXgLh_fyZS4coiwvAt_0wzSl5QoaCaynxpWq7MveizMqfLfMSa_VNa8tyKwGsBz/pub?start=false&loop=false&delayms=3000)

## Native Areas vs. Traditional Areas of the Golf Couse

Native areas, or natural areas, are unique parts of the golf course that are maintained much differently than traditional parts of the course, such as tee boxes, fairways, rough, and greens. These traditional areas of the course are intensively maintained, meaning they are irrigated and mowed frequently and receive regular scheduled fertilization throughout the year.

Native areas, on the other hand, are maintained much less frequently. Native areas are almost entirely non-irrigated parts of the course, meaning they only receive water from rain and snow, with the exception of when the golf maintenance team is actively trying to establish native grasses or plants in a particular area of the course. In that instance, that native area may receive minor irrigation to allow those plants to mature and become self-sustaining.

![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=3470)

## Where are native areas?

Native areas often act as a boundary for a golf hole and are considered “out of play” for golfers. Native areas are frequently located between private properties and the “traditional” areas of the course. These areas of the course are where vegetation is allowed to grow to mature lengths.

![](/ImageRepository/Document?documentId=3471)

## Mowing Frequency of Native Areas

Native areas on the golf course follow a similar mowing schedule as the [City’s Open Space, greenways and trail corridors](/517).

- Courtesy Cuts along property fence lines are completed three to five times a summer
- Vegetation along property lines are mowed to approximately 5 to 8 inches in height and are a minimum of 6 feet wide
- Courtesy Cuts are completed in areas of the course where our equipment can reach
- It’s important to point out that, particularly during the spring, native areas are intentionally mowed to promote growth; so it’s not uncommon to see these Courtesy Cut areas regrow quickly and return to the height they were mowed, sometimes as quickly as two weeks after mowing
- All other native areas are mowed twice a year – once in the spring around Memorial Day, and again in the late fall or early winter
